Had I listened to my accountant, I'd not be in this mess now.
I wouldn't be in this mess now had I listened to my accountant.
I'd not be in this mess now had I listened to my accountant.
why: Inversion: *Had* + subject + past participle replaces *if I had* + past participle.

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct: Hadn't I taken that job, I wouldn't be living here now.
wrong: Had I not taken that job, I wouldn't be living here now.
Had I taken that job, I would be rich now.
Were I braver, I would have said no.
why: Negative inversion is *Had I not ...*, not *Hadn't I ...*

q: You write a formal report about a past failure with a present effect. Choose the correct option.
correct: Had the contract been checked properly, we would not be facing these penalties now.
wrong: If the contract had checked properly, we would not be facing these penalties now.
Had the contract been checked properly, we wouldn't facing these penalties now.
Had checked the contract properly, we would not be facing these penalties now.
why: Passive inversion: *Had* + object + *been* + past participle.

q: Write a mixed conditional with inversion about a past decision and its effect today. Start with Had I.
model: Had I saved more when I was young, I would be more relaxed about money today.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

q: Which sentence means the same as 'If you should need any help, call me'?
correct: Should you need any help, call me.
wrong: Did you need any help, call me.
Would you need any help, call me.
Need you any help, call me.
why: *Should* + subject + base verb is a formal way to say *if you should ...*

q: What does 'unless' mean in 'We'll start unless it rains'?
correct: if it does not rain
why: *Unless* = *if ... not.*

q: Rewrite with unless: You will not get a refund if you don't have a receipt.
answers: You will not get a refund unless you have a receipt.
Unless you have a receipt, you will not get a refund.
why: *Unless* replaces *if ... not*, so the verb after *unless* is positive.
hints: After *unless* we do not use a negative: *... unless you have a receipt.*

q: Which sentence means the same as: 'If you don't hurry, we will miss the flight.'?
correct: Unless you hurry, we will miss the flight.
wrong: If you hurry, we will miss the flight.
Unless you hurry, we will catch the flight.
We will catch the flight unless you hurry.
why: *Unless you hurry* means *if you do not hurry*, so the warning stays the same: we will miss the flight. The other sentences change who must hurry or what happens.

q: Choose the most formal option.
correct: Should you require further information, please contact our office.
wrong: If you want more info, ring us.
If you need more information, just call us.
Call us if you need more info.
why: *Should* + subject + verb is formal and common in business letters.

q: Write a sentence with 'provided that' or 'as long as' to give a condition for a favour.
must: \b(provided that|providing that|as long as|so long as)\b
model: You can borrow my laptop as long as you bring it back by Friday.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

q: Which sentence expresses regret about the present?
correct: I wish I lived closer to the sea.
wrong: I wish I had lived closer to the sea.
I wish I will live closer to the sea.
I wish I would live closer to the sea.
why: *wish* + past simple = regret about a present situation.

q: 'I wish you would stop clicking your pen.' What does 'wish + would' show?
correct: annoyance about someone's repeated behaviour
why: *wish* + *would* is for things that annoy us and that we want to change.

q: I wish I ___ that email yesterday. Now everyone knows.
answers: hadn't sent
why: *wish* + past perfect = regret about the past.

q: Which sentence has a mistake?
correct: If only I would have saved more money when I was young.
wrong: If only I had saved more money when I was young.
I wish I had saved more money when I was young.
If only I saved more money now.
why: *If only* + past perfect is used for regret about the past. Not *would have.*

q: You give a speech about a past failure. Choose the correct option.
correct: If only we had listened to the warning signs, we would not be in this position.
wrong: If only we would have listened to the warning signs, we would not be in this position.
If only we listened to the warning signs, we would not be in this position.
If only we had listen to the warning signs, we would not be in this position.
why: *If only* + *had* + past participle, then *would* + base verb for the present result.

q: Write a sentence with 'I wish' or 'If only' about something you regret from last year.
must: For a regret about the past use the past perfect (*had / hadn't*).
model: I wish I had started learning Spanish last year.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

q: Report it. Move the verb one step back: 'I am tired,' she said. → She said she ___ tired.
correct: was
why: In reported speech the verb usually goes one step back in time: *am / is → was.*

wrong_why.is: *Is* can stay when the information is still true now, but this task asks you to move the verb one step back: *was*.
wrong_why.will be: This changes the statement to a future meaning; it does not backshift *am*.

why_lv: Netiešajā runā darbības vārds parasti iet vienu soli atpakaļ laikā: *am / is → was*.

wrong_why_lv.is: *Is* var saglabāt, ja informācija joprojām ir aktuāla, bet šajā uzdevumā jāveic laiku saskaņošana uz *was*.
wrong_why_lv.will be: Tas maina nozīmi uz nākotni, nevis saskaņo *am* pagātnē.

q: Match each sentence with its report.
pairs: 'I work in a bank,' she said.
She said she worked in a bank.
'I'm working late,' she said.
She said she was working late.
'I finished the report,' she said.
She said she had finished the report.
'I can come,' she said.
She said she could come.
why: With a past reporting verb the tense often goes one step back: *work → worked, am working → was working, finished → had finished, can → could.* It is not always needed, for example when the fact is still true.
why_lv: Pēc darbības vārda pagātnē laiks bieži iet vienu soli atpakaļ: *work → worked, am working → was working, finished → had finished, can → could*. Tas nav vienmēr vajadzīgs, piemēram, ja fakts joprojām ir patiess.

q: 'I don't like coffee,' Mark said. → Mark said he ___ coffee. (not / like)
answers: didn't like
did not like
why: The present simple moves back to the past simple: *don't like → didn't like.*
hints: In reported speech the present simple becomes the past simple: *he didn't like.*
Netiešajā runā Present Simple kļūst par Past Simple: *he didn't like*.
why_lv: Present Simple pāriet uz Past Simple: *don't like → didn't like*.

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct: He said me he was tired.
wrong: He told me he was tired.
He said to me that he was tired.
why: After *said* we do not use a person directly. Use *told me*, or *said to me.*
why_lv: Pēc *said* personu tieši nelieto. Lieto *told me* vai *said to me*.

q: Report this: 'I can't come to the meeting,' Jon said. Choose the correct option.
correct: Jon said he couldn't come to the meeting.
wrong: Jon said I couldn't come to the meeting.
Jon said he can't came to the meeting.
Jon said he couldn't to come to the meeting.
why: *can't → couldn't*, and *I → he* (Jon is talking about himself).
why_lv: *can't → couldn't*, un *I → he* (Jons runā par sevi).

q: Report this sentence. 'I'm learning Spanish,' Elena said. Start with Elena said.
model: Elena said she was learning Spanish.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.
why_lv: Salīdzini savu teikumu ar piemēra atbildi.

q: Use backshift. Direct: 'I have finished.' Reported: He said he ___ finished.
correct: had
why: The present perfect (*have finished*) goes back to the past perfect (*had finished*).
why_lv: Present Perfect (*have finished*) pāriet uz Past Perfect (*had finished*).

q: What usually happens to 'tomorrow' and 'now' in reported speech?
correct: They change to 'the next day' and 'then'.
why: Time words move too: *now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the day before.*
why_lv: Mainās arī laika vārdi: *now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, yesterday → the day before*.

q: Report this: 'I'm leaving now,' Kate said.
answers: Kate said she was leaving then.
Kate said that she was leaving then.
Kate said she was leaving at that moment.
Kate said that she was leaving at that moment.
Kate said she was leaving at that time.
Kate said that she was leaving at that time.
Kate said she was leaving right then.
Kate said she was leaving now.
Kate said that she was leaving now.
Kate said she was leaving.
Kate said that she was leaving.
why: *I → she, am leaving → was leaving, now → then.*
hints: *Now* parasti kļūst par *then* vai *at that moment*.
why_lv: *I → she, am leaving → was leaving, now → then.*

q: You are reporting past statements using backshift. Which sentence has NOT backshifted its future verb?
correct: She said she will call me the next day.
wrong: She said she would call me the next day.
She told me she had finished the report.
He said he was working at home that day.
why: Only this sentence keeps *will*. With backshift it is: *She said she would call me the next day.*
why_lv: Tikai šajā teikumā paliek *will*. Ar laiku saskaņošanu tas ir: *She said she would call me the next day.*

q: You report a message to your manager: 'We are almost ready,' the team said. Choose the correct option.
correct: The team told me they were almost ready.
wrong: The team told me we were almost ready.
The team said me they were almost ready.
The team told they were almost ready.
why: *told* needs a person (*told me*). *We* becomes *they*, and *are* goes back to *were.*
why_lv: *told* vajag personu (*told me*). *We* kļūst par *they*, un *are* pāriet uz *were*.

q: Report what a colleague said yesterday: 'I'll send the file tomorrow.' Start with He said.
must: \b(the next day|the following day|today|that day|the day after)\b
model: He said he would send the file the next day.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.
why_lv: Salīdzini savu teikumu ar piemēra atbildi.

q: Put the words in order.
sentence: she said she was leaving at six that day
answers: she said she was leaving at six that day
she said she was leaving that day at six
why: Reported speech: *said* + subject + backshifted verb. *Today* becomes *that day.*
why_lv: Netiešā runa: *said* + teik. priekšmets + darbības vārds, kas iet soli atpakaļ. *Today* kļūst par *that day*.

q: Which modal normally stays in the same form when we backshift a report?
correct: might
why: *can → could, will → would, must → had to.* *Might, would, could, should* and *ought to* stay the same.

q: 'The Earth goes round the Sun,' the teacher said. Why can we report it as 'The teacher said the Earth goes round the Sun'?
correct: Because it is still true.
wrong: Because said is in the past.
Because reported speech never changes the tense.
Because goes is an irregular verb.
why: When a fact is still true, the tense does not have to go back: *The teacher said the Earth goes round the Sun.*

q: Report this: 'You must finish by Friday,' my boss said.
answers: My boss said I had to finish by Friday.
My boss said that I had to finish by Friday.
My boss told me I had to finish by Friday.
My boss told me that I had to finish by Friday.
My boss said I must finish by Friday.
My boss told me I must finish by Friday.
My boss said that I must finish by Friday.
My boss told me that I must finish by Friday.
why: *must* can become *had to.* It can also stay *must* when the duty is still there.

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct: She told that she would be late.
wrong: She said that she would be late.
She told me that she would be late.
She told us she would be late.
why: *tell* is always followed by a person: *She told me / us ...*

q: Report this naturally: 'I won't sign it until the lawyer reads it,' the client said. Choose the correct option.
correct: The client said he wouldn't sign it until the lawyer had read it.
wrong: The client said he won't sign it until the lawyer will read it.
The client said I wouldn't sign it until the lawyer reads it.
The client told he wouldn't sign it until the lawyer read it.
why: *won't → wouldn't, I → he*, and the earlier action goes back to the past perfect.

q: Report a warning from your doctor: 'You must drink more water.' Start with My doctor said.
model: My doctor said I had to drink more water.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

q: Choose the correct option: 'Where do you work?' She asked me ___.
correct: where I worked
why: In a reported question we use normal word order (subject + verb) and no *do / does / did.*
why_lv: Netiešajā jautājumā lieto parasto vārdu secību (teik. priekšmets + darbības vārds) un bez *do / does / did*.

q: Which word(s) do we use to report a yes/no question?
correct: if or whether
why: *Do you like jazz?* → *He asked if (or whether) I liked jazz.*
why_lv: *Do you like jazz?* → *He asked if* (vai *whether*) *I liked jazz.*

q: Report with backshift: 'What time does the film start?' → She asked what time the film ___. (start)
answers: started
why: Reported question: normal word order, the verb goes back to the past: *started.*
hints: No *does* or *did* in a reported question: *... what time the film started.*
Netiešajā jautājumā nav *does* vai *did*: ... *what time the film started*.
why_lv: Netiešais jautājums: parasta vārdu secība, darbības vārds iet atpakaļ pagātnē: *started*.

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct: He asked me where did I live.
wrong: He asked me where I lived.
He asked if I wanted a coffee.
She asked whether it was true.
why: A reported question has statement word order: *where I lived*, not *where did I live.*
why_lv: Netiešajam jautājumam ir teikuma vārdu secība: *where I lived*, nevis *where did I live*.

q: A hotel guest asked: 'Is breakfast included?' You report the question. Choose the correct option.
correct: The guest asked whether breakfast was included.
wrong: The guest asked was breakfast included.
The guest asked that breakfast was included.
The guest asked is breakfast included.
why: Yes/no question: *asked* + *if / whether* + subject + verb.
why_lv: Jā/nē jautājums: *asked + if / whether* + teik. priekšmets + darbības vārds.

q: Report this question: 'Why are you leaving?' Start with Kate asked me why.
must: Statement word order: *why I was leaving.*
Teikuma vārdu secība: *why I was leaving*.
model: Kate asked me why I was leaving.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.
why_lv: Salīdzini savu teikumu ar piemēra atbildi.

q: Which sentence reports the request 'Please wait here,' the guard said?
correct: The guard told me to wait there.
wrong: The guard told me wait there.
The guard told me that I wait here.
The guard said me to wait there.
why: Orders and requests: *told / asked* + person + *to* + base verb. *Here* becomes *there.*
why_lv: Rīkojumi un lūgumi: *told / asked* + persona + to + pamatforma. *Here* kļūst par *there*.

q: Put the words in order.
sentence: she asked me where I lived
answers: she asked me where I lived
why: Reported question: *asked* + question word + subject + verb.
why_lv: Netiešais jautājums: *asked* + jautājamais vārds + teik. priekšmets + darbības vārds.

q: Put the words in order.
sentence: he asked if I had finished the report
answers: he asked if I had finished the report
why: Yes/no question: *asked* + *if* + subject + verb.
why_lv: Jā/nē jautājums: *asked + if* + teik. priekšmets + darbības vārds.

q: Which report is correct? 'Can you help me?' she asked.
correct: She asked if I could help her.
wrong: She asked if could I help her.
She asked can I help her.
She asked that I could help her.
why: *can → could, you → I, me → her*, and statement word order after *if.*

q: 'Don't touch that!' the nurse said. Which report is correct?
correct: The nurse told me not to touch it.
wrong: The nurse told me to not touching it.
The nurse told me that I don't touch it.
The nurse said me not to touch it.
why: A negative order: *told* + person + *not* + *to* + base verb.

q: Report this: 'Could you send me the invoice?' Lena asked.
answers: Lena asked me to send her the invoice.
Lena asked if I could send her the invoice.
Lena asked whether I could send her the invoice.
Lena asked me if I could send her the invoice.
Lena asked me whether I could send her the invoice.
Lena asked me to send the invoice to her.
Lena asked if I would send her the invoice.
Lena asked whether I would send her the invoice.
Lena asked me if I would send her the invoice.
Lena asked me whether I would send her the invoice.
Lena asked if I could send the invoice to her.
Lena asked me if I could send the invoice to her.
why: A request can be reported with *asked* + person + *to* + base verb, or with *if / whether* + *could.*

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct: He asked me what time was it.
wrong: He asked me what time it was.
He asked me when the train left.
He asked me if I knew the way.
why: In a reported question the subject comes before the verb: *what time it was.*

q: You report a customer's question to your team: 'How long will the repair take?' the customer asked. Choose the correct option.
correct: The customer asked how long the repair would take.
wrong: The customer asked how long would the repair take.
The customer asked how long will the repair take.
The customer asked how long did the repair take.
why: Normal word order, and *will* goes back to *would.*

q: Report a request you received at work: 'Could you call the supplier?' Start with My manager asked me.
must: \bto call\b|\bif i could call\b|\bwhether i could call\b
Use *to call*, or *if / whether I could call.*
model: My manager asked me to call the supplier.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

q: Which report is correct? 'What should I do?' he asked me.
correct: He asked me what to do.
wrong: He asked me what should he do.
He asked me what he does.
He asked me what to doing.
why: A reported question has statement word order, so *what should he do* is wrong. The report *what to do* is correct here; *what he should do* is also possible.

q: 'Where should I park?' she asked me. Which report is correct?
correct: She asked me where she should park.
wrong: She asked me where should she park.
She asked me where she should to park.
She asked me where did she should park.
why: Statement word order after the question word: *where she should park*. *I* becomes *she*, because she asks about herself.

q: Report this: 'Where should we meet?' they asked.
answers: They asked where they should meet.
They asked where to meet.
why: Statement word order: *where they should meet*. They ask about themselves, so *we* becomes *they*.

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct: She asked me whether or not did I agree.
wrong: She asked me whether or not I agreed.
She asked me whether I agreed or not.
why: After *whether* we use statement word order: *whether or not I agreed.*

q: You write meeting minutes: 'Has the budget been approved?' Ms Novak asked. Choose the correct option.
correct: Ms Novak asked whether the budget had been approved.
wrong: Ms Novak asked has the budget been approved.
Ms Novak asked whether had the budget been approved.
Ms Novak asked that the budget had been approved.
why: Yes/no question: *asked* + *whether* + subject + verb. The present perfect goes back to the past perfect.

q: Report this question using whether. 'Is the data accurate?' the editor asked. Start with The editor asked whether.
must: Use statement word order and the past: *the data was accurate.*
model: The editor asked whether the data was accurate.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

q: Which sentence reports 'I'm sorry I'm late' with a reporting verb?
correct: He apologised for being late.
wrong: He apologised that he was late.
why: *apologise for* + -ing.

q: Match each sentence with the best reporting verb.
pairs: 'I'll definitely be there on time,' she said.
promised
'Don't touch the red button!' he said.
warned
'Why don't we try the new café?' she said.
suggested
'Yes, I broke the vase,' he said.
admitted
why: A reporting verb shows what the speaker did: *promise, warn, suggest, admit.*

q: Report with the verb deny: 'I didn't take your phone,' Max said.
answers: Max denied taking my phone.
Max denied taking your phone.
Max denied that he had taken my phone.
Max denied having taken my phone.
Max denied that he took my phone.
Max denied that he had taken your phone.
Max denied taking the phone.
Max denied that he had taken the phone.
Max denied that he took the phone.
Max denied having taken the phone.
why: *deny* + -ing, or *deny* + *that* + clause.

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct: She suggested to go by train.
wrong: She suggested that we go by train.
She suggested we should go by train.
why: *suggest* is not followed by *to* + base verb. Use -ing or *that* + clause.

q: Report a polite refusal: 'No, I won't work this weekend,' Sam said. Choose the correct option.
correct: Sam refused to work that weekend.
wrong: Sam refused that he works this weekend.
Sam refused me to work that weekend.
why: *refuse* + *to* + base verb.

q: Report this apology with apologise: 'Sorry I forgot the meeting,' Dana said.
model: Dana apologised for forgetting the meeting.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

q: Which sentence reports 'You broke the printer!' as an accusation?
correct: She accused me of breaking the printer.
wrong: She accused me to break the printer.
She accused me that I broke the printer.
She accused me for breaking the printer.
why: *accuse* + person + *of* + -ing.

q: What is the difference? A: 'He insisted on paying.' B: 'He offered to pay.'
correct: A means he would not let others pay. B is a polite offer.
wrong: A is a polite offer and B is a demand.
A is about the past and B about the future.
why: *insist on* = refuse to accept a different decision. *offer* = suggest you will do something.

q: Report with congratulate: 'Well done on winning the award!' Tim said to Jo.
answers: Tim congratulated Jo on winning the award.
Tim congratulated Jo for winning the award.
why: *congratulate* + person + *on* + -ing.

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct: He blamed me for to lose the file.
wrong: He blamed me for losing the file.
He accused me of losing the file.
why: *blame* + person + *for* + -ing.

q: Report this concisely and naturally: 'I'm very sorry for the delay, and I will make sure it never happens again,' the manager said. Choose the correct option.
correct: The manager apologised for the delay and promised that it would not happen again.
wrong: The manager said that he was very sorry for the delay and he will make sure it never happens again.
The manager apologised the delay and promised that it will not happen again.
The manager apologised for the delay and promised to that it would not happen again.
why: A reporting verb says what the speaker did. *apologise for* + noun, *promise* + *that* + clause.

q: Report with a suitable reporting verb. 'It wasn't me who broke it!' said Leo.
must: Use a reporting verb such as *denied* or *insisted.*
model: Leo denied breaking it.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

q: Which sentence reports 'If I were you, I'd take the earlier train,' she said?
correct: She advised me to take the earlier train.
wrong: She suggested me to take the earlier train.
She insisted me to take the earlier train.
She advised to me take the earlier train.
why: *advise* + person + *to* + base verb.

q: 'I'm not going to tell you who did it,' the officer said. Which reporting verb shows he said no?
correct: refused
why: *refuse (to* + base verb*)* means to say no.

q: Report with a suitable reporting verb: 'You really should see a doctor about that cough,' my sister said.
answers: My sister advised me to see a doctor about that cough.
My sister urged me to see a doctor about that cough.
My sister told me to see a doctor about that cough.
My sister encouraged me to see a doctor about that cough.
My sister recommended that I see a doctor about that cough.
My sister recommended that I should see a doctor about that cough.
My sister suggested that I see a doctor about that cough.
My sister suggested that I should see a doctor about that cough.
My sister suggested seeing a doctor about that cough.
My sister suggested I see a doctor about that cough.
My sister suggested I should see a doctor about that cough.
My sister recommended seeing a doctor about that cough.
My sister recommended I see a doctor about that cough.
My sister recommended I should see a doctor about that cough.
My sister advised seeing a doctor about that cough.
My sister advised that I see a doctor about that cough.
My sister advised that I should see a doctor about that cough.
My sister said I should see a doctor about that cough.
My sister said that I should see a doctor about that cough.
My sister told me I should see a doctor about that cough.
My sister told me that I should see a doctor about that cough.
why: *advise / urge / tell / encourage* + person + *to* + base verb; *recommend / suggest / advise* + *-ing* or + *that* + subject + base verb; or *said / told me* + *I should* + base verb.

q: Which sentence has a mistake?
correct: He recommended to reading the report carefully.
wrong: He recommended reading the report carefully.
He recommended that I read the report carefully.
He advised me to read the report carefully.
why: Use *recommended reading* or *recommended that I read*. *Recommended to reading* is not a grammatical verb pattern.

q: You report a complaint in formal English: 'The service was terrible and nobody apologised,' the customer said. Choose the correct option.
correct: The customer complained that the service had been terrible and that nobody had apologised.
wrong: The customer complained about the service had been terrible.
The customer complained to be terrible the service.
The customer complained me that the service was terrible.
why: *complain* + *that* + clause. The past goes back to the past perfect.

q: Report with a suitable reporting verb and a noun phrase: 'Thank you for everything you've done,' Mia said to the team.
model: Mia thanked the team for everything they had done.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

q: Choose the correct sentence.
correct: Could you tell me where the station is?
wrong: Could you tell me where is the station?
Could you tell me where's the station is?
Could you tell me where the station?
why: After *Could you tell me* we use statement word order: *where the station is.*
why_lv: Pēc *Could you tell me* lieto teikuma vārdu secību: *where the station is*.

q: Match each direct question with its polite, indirect form.
pairs: Where is the toilet?
Do you know where the toilet is?
What time does the bank open?
Could you tell me what time the bank opens?
How much is this?
Can you tell me how much this is?
Is the shop open?
I wonder if the shop is open.
why: An indirect question starts with a polite phrase, then uses statement word order (no *do / does*).
why_lv: Netiešais jautājums sākas ar pieklājīgu frāzi, tad seko teikuma vārdu secība (bez *do / does*).

q: Where does Anna live? → Do you know where Anna ___?
answers: lives
why: In an indirect question there is no *does*: *where Anna lives.*
hints: No *does* in the indirect part: *... where Anna lives.*
why_lv: Netiešajā jautājumā *does* nav: *where Anna lives*.

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct: Do you know what time does the film start?
wrong: Do you know what time the film starts?
Could you tell me where she lives?
I wonder how much it costs.
why: No *does* after the question word in an indirect question: *what time the film starts.*
why_lv: Netiešajā jautājumā pēc jautājamā vārda nav *does*: *what time the film starts*.

q: You ask a stranger for the post office. Choose the most polite option.
correct: Excuse me, could you tell me where the post office is?
wrong: Tell me where the post office is.
Excuse me, where is the post office?
why: A polite phrase + an indirect question sounds softer and more polite.
why_lv: Pieklājīga frāze + netiešais jautājums skan maigāk un pieklājīgāk.

q: Write a polite indirect question to ask a colleague where the meeting room is. Start with Could you tell me.
must: Start with *Could you tell me where.*
Sāc ar *Could you tell me where.*
Use statement word order: *where the meeting room is.*
Lieto teikuma vārdu secību: *where the meeting room is*.
model: Could you tell me where the meeting room is?
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.
why_lv: Salīdzini savu teikumu ar piemēra atbildi.

q: Put the words in order.
sentence: could you tell me where the station is
answers: could you tell me where the station is
you could tell me where the station is
why: Polite phrase + question word + subject + verb.
why_lv: Pieklājīga frāze + jautājamais vārds + teik. priekšmets + darbības vārds.

q: Put the words in order.
sentence: do you know what time the bank opens
answers: do you know what time the bank opens
why: *Do you know* + question word + subject + verb (no *does*).
why_lv: *Do you know* + jautājamais vārds + teik. priekšmets + darbības vārds (bez *does*).

q: Choose the correct word: Do you know ___ the shop is open on Sundays?
correct: if
why: For a yes/no question inside another question we use *if* or *whether.*
why_lv: Jā/nē jautājumam citā jautājumā lieto *if* vai *whether*.

q: Why is 'Could you tell me where is the station?' wrong?
correct: After 'Could you tell me' we need statement word order: where the station is.
wrong: Because we must use what instead of where.
Because the sentence needs two question marks.
why: In an indirect question the verb comes after the subject.
why_lv: Netiešajā jautājumā darbības vārds ir aiz teikuma priekšmeta.

Palīgteikumā nav *does*: ... *what time the museum closes*.
why_lv: Pieklājīga frāze + *what time* + teik. priekšmets + darbības vārds. Bez *does*.

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?

wrong: Do you know who she is?
Could you tell me if he's here?
why: After *I wonder* we use statement word order: *what she wants.*
why_lv: Pēc *I wonder* lieto teikuma vārdu secību: *what she wants*.

q: You write a polite email to a client. Choose the correct option.
correct: Could you let me know whether the contract has been signed?
wrong: Could you let me know has the contract been signed?
Could you let me know if has the contract been signed?
Could you let me know whether has been the contract signed?
why: *Could you let me know* + *whether / if* + subject + verb.
why_lv: *Could you let me know + whether / if* + teik. priekšmets + darbības vārds.

q: Write an indirect question to ask a stranger whether the café takes cards. Start with Do you know if.
model: Do you know if the café takes cards?
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.
why_lv: Salīdzini savu teikumu ar piemēra atbildi.

q: Put the words in order.
sentence: I wonder what time the meeting starts
answers: I wonder what time the meeting starts
why: *I wonder* + question word + subject + verb.
why_lv: *I wonder* + jautājamais vārds + teik. priekšmets + darbības vārds.

q: Which sentence is correct and polite?
correct: Would you mind telling me how long the repair will take?
wrong: Would you mind telling me how long will the repair take?
Would you mind to tell me how long the repair will take?
Would you mind telling me how long does the repair take?
why: *Would you mind* + -ing, then statement word order.

q: What is the difference? A: 'Where is the manager?' B: 'Do you happen to know where the manager is?'
correct: B is more polite and indirect.
wrong: A is more polite than B.
why: Indirect questions with phrases like *Do you happen to know* sound softer.

q: Make it indirect: Why didn't the order arrive?
answers: Could you tell me why the order didn't arrive?
Do you know why the order didn't arrive?
Can you tell me why the order didn't arrive?

Could you please tell me why the order did not arrive?

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct: I'd like to know where did you put the keys.
wrong: I'd like to know where you put the keys.
Do you remember where you put the keys?
I wonder where I put them.
why: Statement word order after *I'd like to know*: *where you put the keys.*

q: You call customer service. Choose the correct option.
correct: I was wondering if you could tell me when my order will be delivered.
wrong: I was wondering when will my order be delivered?
I was wondering if you could tell me when will my order be delivered?
I was wondering that you could tell me when my order will be delivered.
why: *I was wondering if you could tell me* + *when* + subject + verb.

q: Write a polite indirect question to ask when a report will be ready. Start with I was wondering.
must: Use statement word order: *when the report will be ready.*
model: I was wondering if you could tell me when the report will be ready.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

q: Which is correct? 'I don't know ___.'
correct: what to do
why: Question word + *to* + base verb: *what to do.*

q: 'I have no idea how to start.' What does 'how to start' mean?
correct: how I should start
why: A question word + to-infinitive shows what you do not know how or what to do.

q: Join with a question word + to: I don't know. What should I say?
answers: I don't know what to say.
I do not know what to say.
why: *I don't know* + *what* + *to* + base verb.

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct: I can't decide whether accepting the offer.
wrong: I can't decide whether to accept the offer.
I can't decide whether or not to accept the offer.
I can't decide whether to accept the offer or not.
why: After *whether* we use *to* + base verb, or a full clause.

q: You write a formal email. Choose the correct option.
correct: It remains unclear who is responsible for the delay.
wrong: It remains unclear who is the responsible for the delay.
It remains unclear who responsible is for the delay.
It remains unclear who does responsible for the delay.
why: Embedded question: *who + is + responsible* (statement order).

q: Write a sentence with 'I have no idea' and a question word (how, what, where, when, who or why).
must: Use *I have no idea* + a question word.
model: I have no idea how long the meeting will take.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

q: Which sentence uses an embedded question as the subject?
correct: Whether he will attend remains unclear.
wrong: He asked whether I would attend.
We do not know whether he will attend.
why: *Whether he will attend* expresses an unresolved yes/no question and is the subject of *remains unclear*. In the other statements, the embedded question is not the subject.

The embedded question complements *asked*. The subject of the main clause is *He*.
wrong_why.Will he attend the meeting?: This is a direct question, not a question embedded inside another clause.
The embedded question complements *know*. The subject of the main clause is *We*.

q: 'It depends on whether the budget is approved.' Why whether and not if?
correct: After a preposition we use whether, not if.
wrong: Because the sentence is in the past.
Because if can only start a conditional clause, never a noun clause.
why: after prepositions: depends *on whether*, talk *about whether.*

q: Combine the two sentences without changing their meaning: Who made the decision? It's not clear.
answers: It's not clear who made the decision.
It is not clear who made the decision.
Who made the decision is not clear.
It's unclear who made the decision.
It is unclear who made the decision.
why: Keep the meaning of *It's not clear*. *Who* is the subject of *made*, so use *who made the decision*. *I wonder who made the decision* is grammatical but changes the main idea.

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct: We talked about how could we improve the results.
wrong: We talked about how to improve the results.
We talked about how we could improve the results.
We talked about whether to improve the results.
why: No question order after *about*: *how we could improve the results.*

q: You write a report: 'The question is ___.' Choose the correct option.
correct: whether the project is worth the cost
wrong: is the project worth the cost
if is the project worth the cost
whether is the project worth the cost
why: The question is + *whether* + subject + verb.

q: Write a sentence starting with 'The question is' + whether / how / why + a clause.
must: Start with *The question is* + a question word.
model: The question is whether we can afford the delay.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

q: Choose the correct word: ___ finishes first wins a prize.
correct: Whoever
why: *Whoever* is the subject of *finishes.* It means *any person who.*

q: 'Whatever he says, don't sign it.' What does 'whatever' mean here?
correct: it does not matter what he says
why: *whatever / whoever / wherever* + clause: it does not matter what / who / where.

q: Rewrite with a wh-ever word: It doesn't matter who calls. Don't answer.
answers: Whoever calls, don't answer.
Whoever calls, do not answer.
Don't answer, whoever calls.
Do not answer, whoever calls.
why: *Whoever* + verb = it does not matter who.

q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
correct: Whomever wins the contract will celebrate.
wrong: Whoever wins the contract will celebrate.
Give it to whomever you trust.
Give it to whoever wants it.
why: *Whoever wins*: *whoever* is the subject. In *whomever you trust*, *whomever* is the object.

q: You write a formal report. Choose the correct option.
correct: How the funds were spent remains to be investigated.
wrong: How were the funds spent remains to be investigated.
How the funds were spent it remains to be investigated.
How funds were the spent remains to be investigated.
why: An embedded question used as the subject keeps statement word order.

q: Write a sentence with 'whoever', 'whatever' or 'wherever' to describe a flexible rule at your workplace.
model: You can sit wherever you like.
why: Compare your sentence with the model answer.

q: Put the words in order. Start with My brother.
why: Use *works* with *my brother* (= *he*). Put the subject before the verb: *My brother works*.
sentence: my brother works in a hospital
answers: my brother works in a hospital
display_answer: My brother works in a hospital.
why_lv: Ar *my brother* (= *he*) lieto *works*. Teikuma priekšmetu liek pirms darbības vārda: *My brother works*.

q: Put the words in order. Start with They.
why: The present continuous uses *am/is/are + verb-ing*. With *they*, use *are waiting*.
sentence: they are waiting for the bus
answers: they are waiting for the bus
display_answer: They are waiting for the bus.
why_lv: Present Continuous veido ar *am/is/are* un darbības vārdu ar *-ing*. Ar *they* lieto *are waiting*.

q: Make a question. Start with Did and put yesterday at the end.
why: Past-simple questions use *did + subject + base verb*: *Did you watch*, not *Did you watched*.
sentence: did you watch the film yesterday
answers: did you watch the film yesterday
display_answer: Did you watch the film yesterday?
why_lv: Jautājumā lieto *did*, teikuma priekšmetu un darbības vārda pamatformu: *Did you watch*, nevis *Did you watched*.

q: Put the words in order. Start with She.
why: *Was reading* describes the activity already in progress. *Rang* is the past-simple event that happened during it.
sentence: she was reading when the phone rang
answers: she was reading when the phone rang
display_answer: She was reading when the phone rang.
why_lv: *Was reading* apraksta darbību, kura jau norisinājās. *Rang* ir Past Simple darbība, kas notika tās laikā.

q: Ask about life experience. Start with Have you ever.
why: Use *Have you ever + past participle* to ask about experience without naming a finished past time.
sentence: have you ever visited this museum
answers: have you ever visited this museum
display_answer: Have you ever visited this museum?
why_lv: Lai jautātu par pieredzi, nenorādot konkrētu pabeigtu laiku pagātnē, lieto *Have you ever* un darbības vārda 3. formu.

q: Make a duration question. Start with How long and put here at the end.
why: *How long have you been waiting?* asks about the duration of an activity continuing to now or just finished.
sentence: how long have you been waiting here
answers: how long have you been waiting here
display_answer: How long have you been waiting here?
why_lv: *How long have you been waiting?* jautā par darbības ilgumu. Darbība turpinās līdz tagadnei vai tikko beigusies.

q: Put the words in order. Start with The train.
why: *Had left* places the departure before the past arrival. *Before* also makes the sequence clear.
sentence: the train had left before we arrived
answers: the train had left before we arrived
display_answer: The train had left before we arrived.
why_lv: *Had left* parāda, ka vilciens aizbrauca pirms mūsu ierašanās pagātnē. Arī *before* skaidri norāda secību.

q: Describe a plan. Start with I am going to and put tonight at the end.
why: Use *am going to + base verb* for a plan: *I am going to cook*.
sentence: I am going to cook dinner tonight
answers: I am going to cook dinner tonight
display_answer: I am going to cook dinner tonight.
why_lv: Plānu izsaka ar *am going to* un darbības vārda pamatformu: *I am going to cook*.

q: Make a passive sentence. Start with These bicycles.
why: The bicycles receive the action. A plural subject needs *are + past participle*: *are made*.
sentence: these bicycles are made in Italy
answers: these bicycles are made in Italy
display_answer: These bicycles are made in Italy.
why_lv: Velosipēdi ir tas, ar ko kaut kas tiek darīts. Daudzskaitlī lieto *are* un 3. formu: *are made*.

q: Make a passive sentence. Start with The window.
why: The past passive uses *was/were + past participle*. With *the window*, use *was broken*.
sentence: the window was broken during the storm
answers: the window was broken during the storm
display_answer: The window was broken during the storm.
why_lv: Pagātnes ciešamo kārtu veido ar *was/were* un 3. formu. Ar *the window* lieto *was broken*.

q: Describe work in progress. Start with The road and put this week at the end.
why: *Is being repaired* is the present continuous passive. The work is in progress, and the road receives the action.
sentence: the road is being repaired this week
answers: the road is being repaired this week
display_answer: The road is being repaired this week.
why_lv: *Is being repaired* ir Present Continuous ciešamajā kārtā. Darbs norisinās, un ceļš ir tas, ar ko kaut kas tiek darīts.

q: Ask whether an action is complete. Start with Has and put yet at the end.
why: A present-perfect passive question uses *has/have + subject + been + past participle*.
sentence: has the parcel been delivered yet
answers: has the parcel been delivered yet
display_answer: Has the parcel been delivered yet?
why_lv: Present Perfect ciešamās kārtas jautājumā lieto *has/have*, teikuma priekšmetu, *been* un 3. formu.

q: Make a future passive sentence. Start with The results.
why: Use *will be + past participle* for a future passive: *will be announced*. The results are the focus.
sentence: the results will be announced on Friday
answers: the results will be announced on Friday
display_answer: The results will be announced on Friday.
why_lv: Nākotnes ciešamo kārtu veido ar *will be* un 3. formu: *will be announced*. Uzmanība ir pievērsta rezultātiem.

q: Make a general rule. Start with If.
why: For this general cause-and-effect rule, both clauses use the present simple. In writing: *If you heat butter, it melts.*
sentence: if you heat butter it melts
answers: if you heat butter it melts
display_answer: If you heat butter, it melts.
why_lv: Šajā vispārīgajā cēloņa un seku sakarībā abās daļās lieto Present Simple. Rakstot: *If you heat butter, it melts.*

q: Make a first conditional. Start with If.
why: Use *if + present simple* and *will + base verb* for a possible future: *If it rains, we will stay indoors.*
sentence: if it rains we will stay indoors
answers: if it rains we will stay indoors
display_answer: If it rains, we will stay indoors.
why_lv: Iespējamu nākotnes situāciju izsaka ar *if +* Present Simple un *will* ar pamatformu: *If it rains, we will stay indoors.*

q: Imagine a different present. Start with If I.
why: *Had* describes an imagined present condition, not a past event here. The imagined result uses *would drive*.
sentence: if I had a car I would drive
answers: if I had a car I would drive
display_answer: If I had a car, I would drive.
why_lv: *Had* šeit izsaka iedomātu tagadnes nosacījumu, nevis pagātnes notikumu. Iedomāto rezultātu izsaka *would drive*.

q: Imagine a different past. Start with If I had.
why: Use *had left* for the unreal past condition and *would have caught* for its imagined past result.
sentence: if I had left earlier I would have caught the bus
answers: if I had left earlier I would have caught the bus
display_answer: If I had left earlier, I would have caught the bus.
why_lv: Nereālu pagātnes nosacījumu izsaka *had left*, bet tā iedomāto pagātnes rezultātu — *would have caught*.

q: Link a different past decision to a present result. Start with If I had and put now at the end.
why: *Had studied* imagines a different past decision. *Would be ... now* describes the present consequence.
sentence: if I had studied medicine I would be a doctor now
answers: if I had studied medicine I would be a doctor now
display_answer: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.

q: Make an inverted third conditional. Start with Had I.
why: *Had I known* means *If I had known*. Inversion removes *if* and puts *had* before the subject.
sentence: had I known about the delay I would have called you
answers: had I known about the delay I would have called you
display_answer: Had I known about the delay, I would have called you.

q: Report a past statement using backshift. Start with She said.
why: When backshift is required, *I am tired* becomes *she was tired*. *That* introduces the reported statement.
sentence: she said that she was tired
answers: she said that she was tired
display_answer: She said that she was tired.
why_lv: Ja jāveic laiku saskaņošana, *I am tired* kļūst par *she was tired*. *That* ievada atstāstīto izteikumu.

q: Make a reported yes/no question. Start with He asked me.
why: After *whether*, use statement word order: *I needed help*, not *did I need help*.
sentence: he asked me whether I needed help
answers: he asked me whether I needed help
display_answer: He asked me whether I needed help.
why_lv: Pēc *whether* lieto apgalvojuma vārdu secību: *I needed help*, nevis *did I need help*.

q: Report an apology. Start with She.
why: The pattern is *apologise for + noun or -ing form*: *apologised for missing the meeting*.
sentence: she apologised for missing the meeting
answers: she apologised for missing the meeting
display_answer: She apologised for missing the meeting.

q: Make a polite indirect question. Start with Could you tell me.
why: Inside the indirect question, put the subject before the verb: *where the bank is*.
sentence: could you tell me where the bank is
answers: could you tell me where the bank is
display_answer: Could you tell me where the bank is?
why_lv: Netiešā jautājuma daļā teikuma priekšmets ir pirms darbības vārda: *where the bank is*.

q: Use an embedded yes/no question as the subject. Start with Whether.
why: *Whether the plan will work* is the subject of *remains uncertain*. The embedded question uses statement word order.
sentence: whether the plan will work remains uncertain
answers: whether the plan will work remains uncertain
display_answer: Whether the plan will work remains uncertain.

q: Use the present simple. My sister ___ here, but her friends ___ in another office.
why: *My sister* (= *she*) needs *works*. *Her friends* (= *they*) needs the base form *work*.
answers: works
work
why_lv: Ar *my sister* (= *she*) lieto *works*. Ar *her friends* (= *they*) lieto pamatformu *work*.

q: Look! Anna ___ dinner and we ___ the table.
why: Both actions are happening now. Use *is cooking* with *Anna* and *are setting* with *we*.
answers: is cooking
are setting
why_lv: Abas darbības notiek tagad. Ar *Anna* lieto *is cooking*, bet ar *we* — *are setting*.

q: Yesterday I ___ a bus and ___ to the museum.
why: *Yesterday* places both events in the past. The irregular past forms are *take → took* and *go → went*.
answers: took
went
why_lv: *Yesterday* norāda, ka abas darbības notika pagātnē. Neregulārās formas ir *take → took* un *go → went*.

q: Describe two activities in progress at 9 last night: I ___ while my parents ___ TV.
why: Use *was* with *I* and *were* with the plural subject *my parents*. Both verbs take *-ing*.
answers: was studying
were watching
why_lv: Ar *I* lieto *was*, bet ar daudzskaitļa teikuma priekšmetu *my parents* — *were*. Abiem darbības vārdiem pievieno *-ing*.

q: I have ___ my report, but I have not sent it ___.
why: *Already* says the first action is complete. *Not ... yet* says the second action has not happened up to now.
answers: already finished
yet
why_lv: *Already* norāda, ka pirmā darbība jau ir pabeigta. *Not ... yet* nozīmē, ka otrā darbība līdz šim vēl nav notikusi.

q: I decided yesterday: I ___ a course next month. The phone is ringing — I ___ it!
why: *Am going to start* expresses an existing plan. *I will answer* is an offer made at the moment of speaking.
answers: am going to start
will answer
why_lv: *Am going to start* izsaka iepriekš pieņemtu plānu. *I will answer* ir piedāvājums, kas izteikts runāšanas brīdī.

q: Use the present simple passive. This room ___ every day. The windows ___ once a month.
why: Use *is* for one room and *are* for several windows. The passive needs the past participles *cleaned* and *washed*.
answers: is cleaned
are washed
why_lv: Vienai istabai lieto *is*, bet vairākiem logiem — *are*. Ciešamajā kārtā vajadzīgas 3. formas *cleaned* un *washed*.

q: Use the past simple passive. The parcel ___ yesterday, and the documents ___ this morning.
why: *The parcel* is singular, so use *was delivered*. *The documents* is plural, so use *were signed*.
answers: was delivered
were signed
why_lv: *The parcel* ir vienskaitlī, tāpēc lieto *was delivered*. *The documents* ir daudzskaitlī, tāpēc lieto *were signed*.

q: Use the present continuous passive. Your order ___ now, and the tables ___.
why: The order and tables receive the actions. Use *is/are being + past participle* for passive actions in progress.
answers: is being prepared
are being cleaned
why_lv: Pasūtījums un galdi ir tas, ar ko kaut kas tiek darīts. Pašlaik notiekošai darbībai ciešamajā kārtā lieto *is/are being* un 3. formu.

q: Make a first conditional: If she ___ early, we ___ the bus.
why: After *if*, use the present simple *arrives*. The possible future result is *will catch*.
answers: arrives
will catch
why_lv: Pēc *if* lieto Present Simple formu *arrives*. Iespējamo nākotnes rezultātu izsaka *will catch*.

q: Make a second conditional about an imagined present: If I ___ more free time, I ___ a new language.
why: For this imagined present, use *had* in the condition and *would learn* in the result. *Have/will learn* would express a different, first-conditional meaning.
answers: had
would learn
why_lv: Iedomātam tagadnes nosacījumam lieto *had*, bet rezultātam — *would learn*. *Have/will learn* izteiktu citu nozīmi — First conditional.

q: Make a third conditional about a different past: If we ___ earlier, we ___ the train.
why: The unreal past condition needs *had left*. Its imagined past result needs *would have caught*.
answers: had left
would have caught
why_lv: Nereālam pagātnes nosacījumam vajag *had left*. Iedomātajam pagātnes rezultātam vajag *would have caught*.

q: Match each sentence to its meaning.
why: *Every day* signals the habit here. *Am walking* describes now; *walked ... yesterday* describes a finished past event.
pairs: I walk to work every day.
A regular habit.
I am walking to work now.
An action in progress now.
I walked to work yesterday.
A finished action yesterday.
why_lv: *Every day* šeit norāda uz ieradumu. *Am walking* apraksta tagadni, bet *walked ... yesterday* — pabeigtu pagātnes notikumu.

q: Match each sentence to what it expresses.
why: Time expressions help distinguish the uses. The present continuous can describe a temporary situation or a future arrangement.
pairs: I work in the office every Monday.
My regular routine.
I am working from home this week only.
A temporary situation around now.
I am meeting Eva at the café at six tomorrow.
An arrangement for tomorrow.
why_lv: Laika norādes palīdz atšķirt nozīmes. Present Continuous var aprakstīt pagaidu situāciju vai norunātu nākotnes darbību.

q: Match each base verb to its past-simple form.
why: These verbs are irregular: *bring → brought*, *choose → chose*, *leave → left*, *meet → met*. Do not add *-ed*.
pairs: bring
brought
choose
chose
leave
left
meet
met
why_lv: Šie darbības vārdi ir neregulāri: *bring → brought*, *choose → chose*, *leave → left*, *meet → met*. Nepievieno *-ed*.

q: Compare the verb forms and match each sentence to the timing of the cooking.
why: *Was cooking* gives background in progress; *started* marks the beginning; *had finished* places completion before the arrival.
pairs: When Eva arrived, I was cooking.
Cooking was still in progress at her arrival.
When Eva arrived, I started cooking.
Cooking began at her arrival.
When Eva arrived, I had finished cooking.
Cooking was already complete at her arrival.
why_lv: *Was cooking* apraksta notiekošu fona darbību, *started* — tās sākumu, bet *had finished* — pabeigšanu pirms ierašanās.

q: Match each time expression to the information it gives in its sentence.
why: *For* introduces a duration; *since* introduces a starting point. *Not ... yet* describes something that has not happened up to now.
pairs: I have worked here for three years.
The length of the period: three years.
I have worked here since 2023.
The starting point: 2023.
I have not finished yet.
The action is still incomplete now.
why_lv: *For* ievada ilgumu, bet *since* — sākuma punktu. *Not ... yet* apraksta kaut ko, kas līdz šim vēl nav noticis.

q: Compare what each sentence focuses on.
why: The simple form can focus on completion or quantity. The continuous form focuses on the activity and its duration; it does not by itself say the wall is finished.
pairs: I have painted the wall. It is finished.
Completion of one wall.
I have been painting the wall for an hour.
The duration of the painting activity.
I have painted three walls today.
The number of completed walls.
why_lv: Simple forma var uzsvērt pabeigšanu vai daudzumu. Continuous forma uzsver darbību un tās ilgumu; tā pati par sevi nenorāda, ka siena ir pabeigta.

q: Identify the voice and time in each sentence.
why: In the active sentence, the subject does the action. In the passive sentences, the printer receives it. The auxiliaries distinguish past completion from work in progress.
pairs: The technician repaired the printer.
Past active: the technician is the subject.
The printer was repaired yesterday.
Past passive: the printer is the subject.
The printer is being repaired now.
Present continuous passive: the repair is in progress.
why_lv: Darāmajā kārtā teikuma priekšmets veic darbību. Ciešamajā kārtā printeris ir tas, ar ko kaut kas tika darīts. Palīgdarbības vārdi atšķir pagātnes darbību no pašlaik notiekoša darba.

q: Match each situation with the response that best fits its purpose.
why: Choose the form for the purpose: *will* for this immediate offer, present continuous for the arrangement, and *going to* to highlight visible evidence.
pairs: You decide now to help a colleague with a heavy bag.
I'll carry that for you.
You describe a confirmed appointment for tomorrow.
I'm seeing the dentist at ten.
You predict rain because you can see dark clouds.
It's going to rain.
why_lv: Izvēlies formu atbilstoši nolūkam: *will* šim tūlītējam piedāvājumam, Present Continuous norunai un *going to*, lai uzsvērtu redzamās pazīmes.

q: Match each sentence with the relationship it expresses.
why: *If* introduces the condition for the promise. *Unless* means *if not*. *In case* gives the reason for taking a precaution in advance.
pairs: If you help me, I'll buy you lunch.
A promise depending on your help.
We won't start unless everyone is here.
Everyone being present is necessary for us to start.
I'll take water in case the shop is closed.
A precaution against a possible problem.
why_lv: *If* ievada solījuma nosacījumu. *Unless* nozīmē *if not*. *In case* pamato iepriekš veiktu piesardzības pasākumu.

q: Compare the conditionals and match each sentence to its time and meaning.
why: *Had ... would buy* imagines the present; *have ... will buy* concerns a possible future; *had had ... would have bought* imagines a different past.
pairs: If I had enough money now, I'd buy a car.
An imagined present situation.
If I have enough money next month, I'll buy a car.
A possible future situation.
If I had had enough money yesterday, I'd have bought a car.
An imagined alternative to the past.
why_lv: *Had ... would buy* izsaka iedomātu tagadni, *have ... will buy* — iespējamu nākotni, bet *had had ... would have bought* — iedomātu pagātni.

q: Match each statement by Eva to its report. Use backshift.
why: In these backshifted reports, *am → was*, *have finished → had finished*, and *can → could*. Eva becomes *she*.
pairs: 'I am busy,' Eva said.
Eva said she was busy.
'I have finished,' Eva said.
Eva said she had finished.
'I can help,' Eva said.
Eva said she could help.
why_lv: Saskaņojot laikus šajos teikumos, *am → was*, *have finished → had finished* un *can → could*. Evas vietā lieto *she*.

q: Match each direct question to the indirect question with the same meaning.
why: Use statement word order in the indirect part. For a yes/no question, add *if* or *whether*. The auxiliary *does* disappears and the main verb takes *-s*.
pairs: Where is the meeting room?
Could you tell me where the meeting room is?
What time does the café close?
Do you know what time the café closes?
Does this bus stop at the station?
Could you tell me if this bus stops at the station?
why_lv: Netiešajā daļā lieto apgalvojuma vārdu secību. Jā/nē jautājumam pievieno *if* vai *whether*. Palīgdarbības vārds *does* pazūd, un pamatdarbības vārdam pievieno *-s*.
